title: Greedy: Jump Game
oneLiner: Can you reach the last index? Track the farthest index reachable so far in one left-to-right pass.
keyTakeaway: You don't need to know HOW you'd reach an index, only WHETHER you can. Keep farthest, the furthest index any jump so far can land on. If the scan ever reaches an index beyond farthest, you're stuck; otherwise extend farthest with i + nums[i]. One pass, O(n) time, O(1) space.
explanation:
You start at index 0 of nums. nums[i] is the MAXIMUM jump length from index i, so from i you can land on any index from i + 1 to i + nums[i]. Return true if you can reach the last index. For [2, 3, 1, 1, 4] the answer is true (0 to 1, then 1 to 4). For [3, 2, 1, 0, 4] it is false: every route lands on index 3, whose value is 0, and nothing jumps over it.

The brute force tries every jump from every index, which is exponential, or a dynamic programming table ("can I reach the end from i?") filled right to left in O(n^2). The greedy view is simpler. The set of indexes you can reach is always one unbroken block starting at 0: if you can reach index 5, you can reach every index before it too, because the jump that passed over them could have stopped short. So the whole state is one number, farthest, the right edge of that block.

Scan i from 0. If i > farthest, index i can't be reached, and neither can anything after it: return false. Otherwise index i is reachable, so update farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i]). If farthest reaches the last index, return true. Each index is looked at once: O(n) time, two variables of space.

Why is this greedy? At every index it keeps only the best reach and forgets which jumps produced it. That is safe because a bigger reach can only add reachable indexes, never remove them. The follow-up, Jump Game II (next lesson), asks for the FEWEST jumps and needs a little more bookkeeping on the same idea.

The visualization walks [3, 2, 1, 0, 4], the failing example: farthest stalls at 3 and index 4 is never reached.

recognitionSignals: "Can you reach the end?" where each position says how far you may move from it.
Only reachability matters, not the path, so the state collapses to one running maximum.
A DP over positions would work but each cell only asks "is anything to my left reaching me?"
gotchas: nums[i] is the MAXIMUM jump, not an exact jump. Treating it as exact turns this into a graph search and gives wrong answers.
Check i > farthest BEFORE using nums[i]; an unreachable index's value must not extend the reach.
A single-element array is already at the last index: true, even if the value is 0.
confusableWith: Jump Game II (this track) asks for the minimum number of jumps, which is BFS by levels rather than a single running maximum.
Merge Intervals is the same "extend the right edge while the next start is covered" idea, applied to intervals [i, i + nums[i]].

complexity.note: One left-to-right pass keeping a single number, the farthest reachable index.
